Texture-aware diffusion modelling for severity-conditioned synthetic progression-like visualization of diabetic foot ulcers from single images.

abstract.p: Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are serious complications of diabetes associated with delayed healing, infection, and limb amputation. Modelling DFU progression remains challenging because publicly available image datasets generally contain independent single-timepoint images rather than longitudinal follow-up sequences. This study proposes a texture-aware conditional diffusion framework for generating severity-conditioned, progression-like synthetic DFU images from a single RGB input. Instead of claiming patient-specific temporal prediction, the framework models plausible population-level visual transitions across ordinal pseudo-stages derived from clinically relevant severity cues. The full model achieved an SSIM of 0.851 ± 0.020, PSNR of 24.76 ± 1.12 dB, and FID of 44.33 ± 5.02, with higher observed SSIM and PSNR and lower FID values than the evaluated GAN and VAE baselines across structural fidelity and distributional realism. The GAN baseline achieved SSIM 0.782 ± 0.031, PSNR 21.98 ± 1.56 dB, and FID 59.13 ± 6.59, while the VAE baseline achieved SSIM 0.738 ± 0.038, PSNR 19.63 ± 1.83 dB, and FID 69.77 ± 7.44. The framework also obtained a Texture Consistency Score of 0.79 ± 0.04 and a Granulation Tissue Fidelity Score of 0.76 ± 0.05, indicating preservation of fine-grained texture and granulation-related appearance patterns. Ablation results confirmed the contribution of texture conditioning and cross-attention to image fidelity. Advanced severity-state analysis produced SSIM values of 0.674, 0.804, and 0.726 across three pseudo-stages, supporting severity-aligned structural consistency. Since true longitudinal future-state images were unavailable, these metrics indicate synthetic image fidelity and distributional realism, not longitudinal progression accuracy. Longitudinal DFU cohorts and larger clinician-centred validation remain necessary before clinical decision-support use or temporal progression claims can be justified. To assess generalization beyond the primary 493-image dataset, external validation was additionally performed on an independent DFU dataset under a zero-shot setting, demonstrating stable cross-dataset performance with only modest degradation in image fidelity and texture consistency. Therefore, the proposed framework should be interpreted as modelling cross-sectional severity-conditioned appearance interpolation across independent cases, rather than true patient-specific future progression prediction.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are a critical and frequent complication of diabetes, frequently leading to chronic wounds, infection, and even limb amputation if not identified and treated early[1]. The precise forecasting of diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) progression and the risk of recurrence remains a major and complex challenge for clinicians and wound care experts. This challenge is due to the fact that traditional assessment techniques often rely heavily on subjective visual inspection or fixed risk factors that may differ significantly across practitioners and time. Consequently, these traditional methods may not provide sufficiently accurate or reliable assessments, which highlights the necessity of more accurate and objective instruments to enhance patient outcomes [2,3]. Recent computational methods have quickly improved the discipline, using machine learning and deep neural networks to automatically detect, stage, and predict the outcome of diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs). These advanced methods use a variety of imaging modalities, such as photographic, hyperspectral, and thermographic imaging, to increase diagnostic accuracy, allow earlier intervention, and improve patient outcomes. Consequently, they are becoming an increasingly important part of clinical practice, which can help healthcare professionals better manage this complex condition[4,5]. Machine learning algorithms that have been trained on a mix of both clinical data and image-based features, including Random Forests, Support Vector Machines (SVMs) and deep neural networks, can now accurately predict important outcomes such as ulcer healing, disease progression and recurrence. As an example, more sophisticated ML algorithms have reached classification rates as high as 92.5%, and cluster-based analysis has improved the performance of various DFU severity levels, such as mild to severe cellulitis and life- or limb-threatening infections [6,7]. These advanced predictive tools are increasingly valuable in personalized treatment planning and improving patient outcomes [1,8]. Asymmetries of texture and temperature have been found to be very effective in detecting pre-ulcerative conditions. Support Vector Machine (SVM) models have demonstrated sensitivities exceeding 95%, indicating strong predictive performance [9].

The analysis of texture has grown to be a more significant component of wound assessment over the last few years. It has been demonstrated that with a combination of well-designed, traditional texture features and deep learning-based features in combination with standard RGB images, wound healing classification and prognosis models can be significantly enhanced in accuracy. This combined method enables the healthcare professional to gain more insight into the nature of the wounds and possibly make more decisions regarding treatment [8,9].

Emerging deep learning models, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), well-tuned ensemble networks, and radiomics-based models are have shown promise in the field. They have demonstrated strong performance, particularly when explicit texture and shape features are analyzed and modelled. As an example, the EfficientNet architecture has reported a validation accuracy of 95% in the classification of healthy skin and ulcerated tissue, which underlines its possible integration into healthcare systems to enable early detection and treatment of ulcerated tissue [10,11]. Likewise, the Dense-ShuffleGCANet model, which is based on DenseNet, uses attention and channel-centric features to learn the heterogeneous visual properties of DFUs,achieving an accuracy of 86.09%, which is higher than that of several state-of-the-art architectures [12]. Moreover, ensemble models and hybrid architectures, including CNNs with support vector machines (SVMs) or K-nearest neighbors (KNNs), have also been shown to be more precise and robust in the classification of infection and ischemia in DFUs [4,13–15]. These advancements are gradually transforming the way we approach complex imaging and diagnostic tasks, providing more accurate and insightful results [16,17]. Recent advances also include the use of attention-driven networks, Siamese neural networks, and vision transformers, which enable multi-class classification and similarity learning for more nuanced DFU categorization, such as distinguishing between infection, ischemia, or both [18,19]. Segmentation models like Mask2former and U-Net have been applied for automated wound boundary detection and tissue classification, supporting detailed grading of ulcer severity and assisting clinicians in treatment planning [20,21]. In addition to mere detection, the clinical community is increasingly focused on predicting progression and recurrence. This can be achieved using both clinical and image-based predictors. Such approaches may support earlier interventions in informing earlier interventions and building more individualized care plans, ultimately leading to better patient outcomes and decreased risk of complications [22,23]. One recent breakthrough in the field is the use of advanced generative models, such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and, more recently, diffusion models. These models are used to generate synthetic wound images and the modelling of wound development with time. The diffusion models, specifically, have demonstrated impressive fidelity to generate images of Diabetic Foot Ulcers (DFUs), and research has shown that even as many as 70 percent of the synthetic images are viewed by clinical professionals as real, which makes them potentially useful in research, training, and diagnostic applications [24]. Notably, current developments in conditional diffusion models have significantly advanced the ability to predict infections from single wound images. These models have since surpassed most of the current state of the art approaches particularly in sensitivity and specificity, which is a significant breakthrough in medical imaging and diagnostic technology [25].

Synthetic medical imaging is currently undergoing a revolution with generative models, which can now not only be augmented to make rare wound classes but can also be simulated in silico to model disease progression. In particular, diffusion models have become an effective framework to create high-fidelity, realistic, and diverse synthetic images of diabetic foot ulcers [24]. These models have outperformed traditional GANs in terms of both realism and the preservation of clinically relevant microstructural details, as validated by wound experts [25]. Recent works also demonstrate the feasibility of using single images to predict future wound progression, leveraging both texture-aware analysis and computational modeling to forecast healing or deterioration [26,27].

Despite these advances, a major gap remains: existing models rarely integrate multi-scale, texture-aware encoding with robust, diffusion-based synthetic progression modelling from single photographic inputs. Addressing this gap, the present study introduces a texture-aware diffusion framework that integrates hand-crafted and deep texture features with conditional generative modelling to synthesize clinically interpretable, progression-like DFU appearances from a single input image. The proposed approach is positioned as a severity-conditioned visualization framework rather than a definitive temporal prediction system, thereby supporting risk-aware interpretation and methodological development under limited longitudinal data availability [14,28,29].

In response to this gap, the present study introduces a texture-aware conditional diffusion framework for severity-conditioned progression-like DFU image synthesis from a single input image. The framework combines local binary pattern descriptors and deep perceptual texture features with a cross-attention-enhanced diffusion architecture to preserve clinically relevant ulcer texture and morphology. Since the available datasets do not contain true longitudinal follow-up images, the proposed pseudo-progression strategy is not intended to represent deterministic patient-specific temporal forecasting. Instead, it provides a weakly supervised approximation of plausible population-level visual transitions across severity-aligned ordinal stages. This distinction is essential for ensuring that the proposed method is interpreted as progression-like synthetic visualization rather than definitive future ulcer prediction.

list-item.p: This study proposes a texture-aware conditional diffusion framework for generating severity-conditioned progression-like DFU images from a single RGB input, addressing the lack of longitudinal DFU image datasets while avoiding claims of deterministic patient-specific temporal prediction.

Introduces a hybrid texture encoding strategy combining local binary patterns and deep perceptual features, resulting in a Texture Consistency Score of 0.79 ± 0.04 and supporting fine-grained microstructural preservation during progression-like DFU synthesis.

Incorporates a cross-attention mechanism within the diffusion model, achieving an FID of 44.33 ± 5.02 and indicating improved alignment with real ulcer image distributions compared with GAN and VAE baselines.

Presents a Granulation Tissue Fidelity Score(GTFS), achieving 0.76 ± 0.05, indicating biologically plausible representation of granulation-related appearance patterns and supporting preliminary visual interpretability.

Performs detailed ablation studies in which the full model showed the most favorable observed metric values among the evaluated configurations, supporting the contribution of texture conditioning and cross-attention to progression-like synthesis quality.

Presents a timestep-wise severity-state analysis to examine how the model preserves structural and textural consistency across synthetic severity-aligned stages, with SSIM scores of 0.674, 0.804, and 0.726 across the evaluated stages.

sec.title: 3. Methodology
sec.p: This paper introduces a diffusion-based synthetic generation framework that incorporates texture information to produce progression-like synthetic images of diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) under different severity conditions. The methodology aims to generate visualisations of possible changes in the appearance of the ulcer from a single input image under weakly supervised conditions, especially in the absence of longitudinal follow-up datasets. The entire pipeline combines image preprocessing, texture feature encoding, and a conditional diffusion architecture to generate morphologic and textural variations at hypothetical pseudo-stages that are aligned with the severity. Each of the phases of the proposed approach is explained in detail in the following subsections, and the details of data collection, preprocessing strategies, texture encoding techniques, model architecture design, training strategies, evaluation protocols, and implementation specifics are shown in Fig 1.

sec.title: 3.1 Phase 1: Data collection
sec.p: In this study, a publicly available dataset comprising 493 high-resolution RGB images of diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) was obtained from Kaggle [30], as seen in Fig 2. All images show a different type of ulcer, with a wide spectrum of ulcer severity and tissue changes from granulation to necrosis and epithelialization. Images were taken in different clinical settings, and therefore under a variety of lighting conditions, foot position and ulcer morphology. No longitudinal follow-up images were available, so each image was considered as a separate case. The dataset was adequate for modelling ulcer texture patterns and morphological characteristics that could be used to create synthetic images of the DFU that mimic progression. However, the dataset did not contain repeated observations of the same ulcer over time, so direct supervision of true ulcer progression over time was not possible.. Thus, pseudo-stages were constructed from cross-sectional severity cues rather than from temporal wound trajectories, to create severity-aligned pseudo-stages. This design decision is recognized as a methodological limitation and the scope of the proposed framework is limited to a progression-like synthesis based on severity, not to a prediction of the future state. The basic dataset is a collection of 493 photos of diabetic foot ulcers from a public Kaggle repository. The data set was split into 345 images used for training, 74 images used for validation and 74 images used for testing (70%, 15%, 15%). There was no overlap among the training, validation, and test subsets, and the split was performed at the image level using a fixed random seed for reproducibility. A fixed train–validation–test split was used in all the baseline, ablation, and comparative experiments to provide fair and consistent model evaluation under the same data conditions. Patient-wise splitting was not possible as patient identifiers were unavailable in the dataset; this is acknowledged as a limitation of the publicly available DFU image collection. It is also noted that the relatively small size of the primary dataset is an important constraint when training a diffusion-based generative model. To prevent overfitting, the same preprocessing, data augmentation, data splitting and evaluation methods were used for all the model variants. However, the small sample size limits the representativeness of the diversity of the DFU presentations and is thus a methodological limitation. It is important to note that in this study the independent single-timepoint images do not offer temporal supervision. Therefore, the severity pseudo-stages should not be used as chronological stages of the same ulcer. Rather, they are cross-sectional severity groupings of independent case based on visual features of the ulcer appearance including size, depth, prevalence of granulation tissue and necrotic coverage. Hence, the pseudo-stages should be interpreted as appearance interpolations that are conditioned by the severity, not as temporal sequences. This definition clarifies the dataset is appropriate for severity-conditioned progression-like synthesis but not for true longitudinal progression prediction.

sec.p: An advanced preprocessing pipeline was used to create a high-fidelity and robust input representation for the diffusion model, going beyond the standard resizing and simple augmentations. The model backbone is implemented as a U-Net architecture equipped with cross-attention mechanisms, facilitating the propagation of multi-scale features and enabling dynamic focus on critical ulcer regions. In each decoding layer, cross-attention modules integrate the texture encoding FT by learning attention weights α that highlight clinically relevant sub-regions, mathematically expressed as equation 8:

This design allows the model to adaptively focus on ulcer structural patterns and their complexity, which may be associated with ulcer severity. Furthermore, a hierarchical skip-connection approach is used to retain low-level spatial details and capture high-level semantic appearance variations, which ensures structural coherence and textural realism of the final synthetic outputs. The diffusion model was additionally extended with an auxiliary feature-consistency loss that is used to enforce the consistency of the intermediate features of the generated images with the features of the original input image, which is important for encouraging biological plausibility in the progression-like synthetic output. The proposed architecture incorporates a texture-conditioned cross-attention mechanism into a powerful diffusion model to tackle the problem of modelling plausible changes in DFU appearance from a single image when considering severity. This allows for the creation of visually interpretable severity-consistent progression-like visualizations that could aid in exploratory risk-aware interpretation, although further validation would be required before clinical use , as shown in Fig 5.

sec.title: 3.5 Phase 5: Training strategy
sec.p: A multi-objective training strategy was carefully designed to effectively learn the complex mappings needed for realistic synthetic images that resemble severity-associated progression-like appearances of diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs). The main goal was to teach the conditional diffusion model to generate high fidelity progression-like DFU images, while maintaining global morphology and fine-grained textural features corresponding to pseudo-stages that reflect severity. However, no real longitudinal images of ulcers were available and a pseudo-progression paradigm was therefore used. This method involved the categorisation of images and the approximate classification into ordinal pseudo-stages using visual indicators of severity such as ulcer size, depth, granulation presence and necrotic coverage. Pseudo-stage labels were defined using a predefined heuristic, appearance-based severity grouping scheme derived from cross-sectional visual characteristics of the ulcer region. Stage 1 (mild) represented predominantly superficial ulcer appearance with pink granulation and minimal slough; Stage 2 (moderate) represented partial-thickness appearance with visible slough or exudate and irregular wound borders; and Stage 3 (severe) represented deeper ulceration with extensive slough and more pronounced tissue damage. Supporting cues included ulcer size, colour, apparent depth, granulation appearance, exudate/slough, and necrotic coverage. These pseudo-stage labels were used only as weak severity-conditioning variables and were not derived from longitudinal follow-up, patient outcomes, or a formal clinician-led annotation or adjudication protocol. Accordingly, they should be interpreted as heuristic severity groupings rather than clinically validated wound grades or temporal progression labels.

The pseudo-progression paradigm should be viewed as a weakly supervised severity-conditioned ordering paradigm, and not as a temporal supervision paradigm. The available DFU images are cross-sectional and do not represent repeated visits from the same patients., so the model does not learn patient-specific wound evolution over chronological time. Instead, it learns population level visual transitions corresponding to the increase or change in ulcer severity. The outputs are thus not predictions of the clinical state of a particular ulcer, but rather plausible appearance-like progressions given the severity-related texture and morphology of the ulcer. The term pseudo-progression is used in this study to denote the severity conditioned ordinal ordering of independent DFU images. It does not indicate genuine temporal progression, patient-level follow-up, or future-state supervision. The pseudo-progression strategy was adopted only as a practical workaround for limited longitudinal data availability. Since the ordinal stages are derived from cross-sectional images belonging to different cases, the training process models severity-associated appearance interpolation across independent patients rather than true patient-specific temporal progression. Accordingly, the generated outputs are described as severity-conditioned progression-like synthetic visualizations, not as future progression predictions.

The Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10-4, weight decay of 10-5, and a batch size of 8 was used to train. The learning rate was gradually decreased using a cosine annealing scheduler for smoother convergence in later training stages. The training was conducted on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU with convergence taking about 40 hours.

Texture conditioning, perceptual loss, and feature-consistency loss were incorporated to minimize texture degradation during synthesis. However, residual smoothing of very-high-frequency boundary details remained visible in the zoomed-in analysis, indicating the need for explicit frequency-aware and boundary-aware texture-refinement strategies in future work.

This thorough multi-objective optimization approach allowed the model to be taught detailed patterns of ulcer appearance, while simultaneously minimizing the structural deviations while maximizing the textural realism. Several measures were also incorporated to reduce overfitting during training, including extensive data augmentation, weight decay, cosine learning-rate scheduling, exponential moving average of model weights, and validation-based monitoring. These strategies were used to improve training stability and generalization under limited data availability. Nevertheless, the dataset size remains modest for diffusion-based generative modelling, and external validation was therefore included to further examine cross-dataset robustness.

The observed residual smoothing of high-frequency boundary details suggests that future training objectives should extend beyond perceptual and feature consistency losses by incorporating frequency-aware losses, high-pass adversarial supervision, and boundary-level patch refinement to explicitly preserve micro-textural structures, as seen in Fig 6.

sec.title: 3.6 Phase 6: Evaluation and validation
sec.p: To evaluate the technical quality and visual plausibility of the progression-like synthetic diabetic foot ulcer images generated by the proposed diffusion model, an evaluation procedure was used that integrated quantitative image-quality metrics, qualitative visual inspection, ablation analysis, and robustness assessment. Quantitative evaluation was conducted using two established image quality metrics: the Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) and the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID). The SSIM metric, defined as equation 13:

Where μx and μy represent mean intensities, σx2 and σy2 denote variances, σxy is the covariance between images x and y, and c1, c2 are stabilizing constants, which were used to evaluate perceptual similarity between generated images and reference pseudo-progression samples. High SSIM values indicate strong structural fidelity and textural coherence, which are essential for clinical interpretability as seen in Fig 7.

sec.p: FID was employed to quantify the distributional similarity between the generated image set and the real dataset, calculated as equation 14:

where (μr, ∑r) and (μg, ∑g) represent the means and covariance matrices of features extracted from a pre-trained Inception network for real (Xr) and generated (Xg) images, respectively. Lower FID scores indicate higher fidelity and better realism. In parallel, qualitative visual inspection was performed to assess the visual plausibility of the generated progression-like synthetic images. The generated outputs were examined for morphological coherence, texture continuity, ulcer-boundary preservation, and the absence of visually unrealistic artefacts. This qualitative inspection was used only to support technical interpretation of the generated images and should not be interpreted as clinician-based validation, diagnostic evaluation, or evidence of clinical decision-support effectiveness. Since no formal specialist review was conducted, no Likert-scale scoring or inter-rater reliability analysis using Cohen’s kappa was performed.

Moreover, visual interpretability was also enhanced by the creation of pixel-level attention maps based on the cross-attention modules of the model, which identified areas most important in generating progression-like synthetic outputs. These attention overlays supported the straightforward interpretation of the clinical aspects, as certain parts of the ulcer and its texture that contributed to the formed outcomes were highlighted. To supplement the quantitative and qualitative visual analyses, an ablation study was conducted to examine the importance of the main architectural components, including the texture conditioning module and cross-attention mechanisms. Comparisons of metrics such as SSIM and FID were made between the variants of the models with and without each of these components, thereby confirming the importance and effect of each design element on the realism of progression-like synthesis. Because no ground-truth future DFU images were available, the evaluation metrics were not used to measure true longitudinal progression accuracy. SSIM and PSNR were used to assess structural and pixel-level similarity between generated outputs and severity-aligned pseudo-progression references. FID was used to measure distributional similarity between generated images and the real DFU image dataset. Therefore, these metrics quantify synthetic image fidelity, texture preservation, and dataset-level realism, rather than chronological progression accuracy or patient-specific future-state prediction. In addition to established image-quality metrics, two task-specific supplementary metrics, namely the Texture Consistency Score (TCS) and Granulation Tissue Fidelity Score (GTFS), were used to evaluate clinically relevant appearance characteristics that are not fully captured by generic image similarity measures. TCS was designed to assess local micro-textural preservation using LBP-based texture similarity, while GTFS was used to estimate the consistency of granulation-related appearance patterns between generated images and algorithmically derived severity-aligned pseudo-reference appearance maps. These metrics were not intended to replace established evaluation standards such as SSIM, PSNR, FID, clinician-led assessment, or prospective clinical validation. Instead, they were used as complementary exploratory indicators for assessing texture preservation and granulation-related visual plausibility in progression-like DFU synthesis.
Since the pseudo-stages are derived from cross-sectional severity grouping, the evaluation assesses synthetic image fidelity and severity-conditioned consistency, not temporal forecasting accuracy.

sec.title: TCS and GTFS formal definition.
sec.p: To improve reproducibility, the Texture Consistency Score (TCS) and Granulation Tissue Fidelity Score (GTFS) were formally defined and computed using explicit algorithmic steps. These metrics were designed as task-specific supplementary indicators for evaluating texture preservation and granulation-related appearance fidelity in severity-conditioned progression-like DFU synthesis. They were not used as standardized clinical validation metrics.

For each generated progression-like image I^iand its corresponding severity-aligned pseudo-reference image Iir, Local Binary Pattern (LBP) maps were first extracted using the same LBP configuration described in the texture encoding stage. The corresponding LBP histograms were then normalized to obtain HLBP(I^i)and HLBP(Iir). where Dχ2(i) denotes the chi-square texture dissimilarity for the ith image pair, B represents the total number of LBP histogram bins, bdenotes the histogram-bin index, and ε is a small numerical constant added to avoid division by zero. A lower value of Dχ2(i) indicates stronger similarity between the local texture distributions of the generated image and the severity-aligned pseudo-reference image.
The image-level Texture Consistency Score was then obtained by applying exponential normalization to the chi-square distance, as shown in equation 16:

where TCSi represents the texture consistency score for the ith generated image. This transformation maps the texture dissimilarity into a bounded similarity score, where values closer to 1 indicate stronger preservation of local micro-textural patterns.
The final Texture Consistency Score was calculated by averaging the image-level TCS values across all N test samples, as expressed in equation 17:

where N denotes the total number of evaluated test samples. Higher TCS values indicate stronger preservation of fine-grained texture patterns, including local tissue roughness, keratinization-like appearance, and necrosis-like texture variation, between generated progression-like images and severity-aligned pseudo-reference images.

sec.title: Derivation of the granulation-related appearance map.
sec.p: The granulation-related appearance map G(I) was implemented as a deterministic, non-learned soft colour-appearance map rather than as the output of a trained tissue-segmentation network. For each preprocessed RGB image I, analysis was restricted to the ulcer-region mask Ωobtained using the same adaptive background-subtraction and dynamic-thresholding procedure described in Section 3.2. The pixels within Ωwere converted from RGB to the CIELAB colour space. Let L*(p), a*(p), and b*(p) denote the lightness, red–green, and yellow–blue components, respectively, at pixel p. Three normalized appearance components were computed as equation 18 &19.
A soft granulation-related appearance response was then obtained as equation 20.

where MΩ(p) is the binary ulcer-region mask. This formulation assigns greater response to relatively red/pink, non-dark, and non-yellow pixels, while suppressing darker necrosis-like and yellow slough-like appearance patterns. To reduce isolated pixel-level variation, the response map was smoothed using a 3×3 Gaussian kernel with σ=1.0, followed by min–max normalization within the ulcer region as equation 21:

Pixels outside the ulcer mask were assigned a value of zero. The identical procedure and parameters were applied independently to both the generated image and its severity-aligned pseudo-reference image before calculation of the soft Dice-based GTFS. Consequently, G(I) represents a reproducible granulation-like chromatic appearance score rather than a clinically validated tissue-segmentation probability map.

For the Granulation Tissue Fidelity Score, the deterministic granulation-related appearance mapping procedure defined above was applied separately to each generated progression-like image and its corresponding severity-aligned pseudo-reference image. Let Gg denote the normalized granulation-related appearance map of the generated image and Gr denote the corresponding map of the pseudo-reference image. Both maps therefore lie within the range [0,1], with larger values indicating stronger granulation-like chromatic appearance within the ulcer-region domain.
The image-level GTFS was computed using a soft Dice similarity formulation, as given in equation 22:

where GTFSi denotes the granulation tissue fidelity score for the ith image pair, p represents the pixel location, Ω denotes the ulcer-region pixel domain, and ε is a small numerical stabilizer. The soft Dice formulation measures the spatial overlap and intensity-level consistency between granulation-related appearance patterns in the generated image and the severity-aligned pseudo-reference image.
The final Granulation Tissue Fidelity Score was obtained by averaging the image-level GTFS values across all N test samples, as shown in equation 23:

Higher GTFS values indicate stronger spatial consistency of granulation-related appearance patterns between generated progression-like images and severity-aligned pseudo-reference images. Since the granulation-related maps were derived algorithmically from the generated and severity-aligned pseudo-reference images rather than from clinician-verified tissue masks, GTFS should be interpreted as a task-specific exploratory measure of granulation-related appearance fidelity rather than as a standardized clinical tissue-validation metric.

Algorithmically, TCS was computed by extracting LBP maps from each generated and pseudo-reference image, converting these maps into normalized histograms, estimating chi-square histogram dissimilarity, transforming this distance into an image-level similarity score, and averaging the scores across the test set. GTFS was computed by deriving deterministic CIELAB-based granulation-related soft appearance maps within the ulcer region for both generated and pseudo-reference images, applying identical Gaussian smoothing and normalization, comparing the resulting maps using soft Dice similarity, and averaging the image-level scores across the test set. This formulation makes both metrics reproducible and clarifies their role as supplementary technical measures for texture preservation and granulation-related appearance fidelity.

Finally, the ability of the model to withstand perturbations was evaluated by adding synthetic noise and/or small occlusions to the input images and observing the stability and consistency of the progression-like output images. The ability to maintain coherent progression-like outputs in the presence of such perturbations further confirmed the robustness of the proposed synthesis framework. As a combination of these three evaluations, the proposed framework was technically effective in generating and visualizing severity-conditioned severity-progression-like DFU appearances from a single image, as shown in Fig 8. It should be noted that the evaluation protocol was developed to evaluate image fidelity, distributional similarity, texture preservation and preliminary visual plausibility. These measures are not clinical efficacy, diagnostic accuracy, treatment benefit or real-world decision-support performance measures. Qualitative assessment has not been formally examined by an expert clinician, and should only be used as a visual plausibility inspection and not as full clinical validation. The proposed framework would need to be assessed in a larger multi-centre clinician evaluation, patient longitudinal follow-up and prospective clinical outcome analysis before it would be considered clinically deployable.

sec.title: 4. Algorithmic summary of the proposed framework
4.1 Implementation details
sec.p: All model development and experimentation were conducted using Python 3.10 and the PyTorch deep learning framework (version 2.0), providing the flexibility and modularity required to implement the custom conditional diffusion architecture and advanced texture-encoding mechanisms.High-efficiency batch-level operations and reproducible geometric and intensity transformations were achieved by using pre-processing and augmentation pipelines implemented with OpenCV and Albumentations library. To ensure generalizable texture and shape representation, the VGG-19 network used for perceptual feature extraction and loss computations was initialized with pre-trained weights on ImageNet and only intermediate layer activations were used without fine-tuning. Local Binary Pattern (LBP) computations were done with scikit-image while feature normalization was done with custom PyTorch modules to ensure smooth integration with the training pipeline. The training and inference were carried out on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU with 24GB of VRAM, ensuring that the high resolution of ulcer images and the large intermediate feature maps could be processed without limitation of memory. The model was trained for 300 epochs with a batch size of 8, with the Adam optimizer and default values for β1 = 0.9 and β2 = 0.999, and an initial learning rate of 10−4. A cosine annealing learning rate scheduler was employed to gradually decrease the learning rate, facilitating smoother convergence towards the later training stages. Weight decay with a coefficient of 10−5 was applied to mitigate overfitting and promote generalization. In order to reduce the variance of the model weights during training and enhance the output quality, the model weights were stored using an exponential moving average (EMA) with a decay factor of 0.999 throughout the training process. To track back and retest if there was divergence or instability, model checkpoints were saved at each epoch. Visualizations of intermediate attention maps and texture were produced after each 10 epochs as qualitative measures of model interpretability and texture fidelity for the progression-like synthesis. All quantitative experiments were automatically repeated with custom Python scripts to ensure consistency and minimize human bias in repeated experiments, such as SSIM and FID evaluations.

sec.title: 4.1.1 Reproducibility and implementation details.
sec.p: All experiments were performed with the same implementation pipeline, promoting reproducibility. All the experimental variants were trained and evaluated using the same preprocessing, architecture configuration and optimization parameters. Data partitioning and model initialisation were done using a fixed random seed to minimise the variance in the results caused by the stochastic factors as shown in Table 1. A diffusion-based U-Net backbone with texture-aware conditioning and cross-attention mechanisms was adopted for the proposed framework. The evaluation protocol and the definition of metrics for all baseline models, ablation variants and external validation experiments were the same as described in Table 2. To facilitate the fair evaluation under the limited dataset setting, the same random seed, preprocessing pipeline, data split, architecture configuration and evaluation protocol were adopted for the proposed model, baseline models, ablation models and external validation experiments. This design allows for reduced experimental variability, and enables the reproduction of the comparison between the model configurations.

The algorithm starts by extracting texture feature encodings from a single pre-processed image of the diabetic foot ulcer and then merges local binary patterns and deep perceptual representations to create a single conditioning map. This texture-aware map is used to inform the subsequent conditional diffusion process, an iterative denoising process that starts with an initialized latent variable and uses learned texture and morphological information to guide the denoising. The final result is a high-fidelity synthetic image that mimics a progression-like ulcer appearance, preserving the global structure and micro-textural details that are important for clinical interpretation, and aligned to the severity of the ulcer.

sec.p: The quantitative evaluation summarized in Table 3 demonstrates the final performance of the proposed texture-aware conditional diffusion framework on the primary held-out test set. The full model achieved an SSIM of 0.851 ± 0.020, indicating strong structural similarity between the generated progression-like synthetic images and the corresponding severity-aligned pseudo-reference images. The FID value of 44.33 ± 5.02 indicates favorable distributional similarity between the generated image set and the real DFU image distribution. In addition, the Texture Consistency Score of 0.79 ± 0.04 demonstrates preservation of local micro-textural characteristics, while the Granulation Tissue Fidelity Score of 0.76 ± 0.05 indicates consistent representation of granulation-related appearance patterns. These values correspond to the same final full-model evaluation reported in Table 5 and Table 7 and therefore do not represent an alternative aggregation or evaluation subset. Since longitudinal future-state images were unavailable, these metrics quantify synthetic image fidelity, structural consistency, texture preservation, and distributional realism rather than patient-specific longitudinal progression accuracy. All these quantitative results add to the technical strength and initial visual plausibility of the proposed framework. However, they do not independently validate clinical applicability, as image similarity metrics cannot measure treatment impact, diagnostic safety, or patient outcome improvement. It is important to clarify that no formal clinician-led expert review was conducted in the present study. Therefore, no Likert-scale scores, Cohen’s kappa values, or expert-agreement statistics are reported in the experimental results. The qualitative results presented in this section are based on visual plausibility inspection, qualitative visual comparisons, attention overlays, heatmaps, and cross-dataset visual inspection. These results are intended to support technical interpretation of synthetic image fidelity, texture preservation, distributional realism, and preliminary visual plausibility, rather than clinician-validated clinical realism or clinical decision-support effectiveness.

sec.title: 5.2 Texture consistency and granulation fidelity assessment
sec.p: The evaluation presented in Table 4 assessed microstructural texture preservation and granulation-related appearance fidelity using two task-specific supplementary metrics: the Texture Consistency Score (TCS) and the Granulation Tissue Fidelity Score (GTFS). TCS was used to measure local texture-pattern similarity through LBP-based histogram analysis, as formally defined in Equations (15)–(17). GTFS was used to estimate the spatial consistency of granulation-related appearance patterns between generated images and algorithmically derived severity-aligned pseudo-reference appearance maps using the soft Dice-based formulation defined in Section 3.6. The obtained TCS value of 0.79 ± 0.04 suggests that the generated progression-like DFU images preserved fine-grained local texture patterns, including tissue roughness, keratinization-like appearance, and necrosis-like texture variation. Similarly, the GTFS value of 0.76 ± 0.05 indicates plausible spatial consistency of granulation-related appearance patterns in the generated images. These findings support preliminary visual plausibility and texture fidelity under controlled experimental conditions. The reliability of TCS and GTFS was assessed indirectly by examining their consistency with established image-quality metrics, ablation behaviour, and external dataset performance. In the ablation study, removal of texture conditioning and cross-attention reduced both TCS and GTFS along with SSIM and FID, indicating that these metrics followed the expected degradation pattern when important architectural components were removed. Similarly, external validation showed only modest reductions in TCS and GTFS under domain shift, suggesting preliminary cross-dataset stability. However, TCS and GTFS should be interpreted as exploratory task-specific indicators rather than standardized clinical evaluation metrics. These scores are not intended to replace established evaluation standards such as SSIM, PSNR, FID, clinician-led assessment, or prospective clinical validation. Further clinician-centred validation, larger clinician-annotated DFU datasets, inter-rater agreement analysis, and comparison with established wound assessment criteria are required before these metrics can be considered broadly reliable or generalizable.

sec.title: 5.3.3 FID variation across diffusion timesteps.
sec.p: Fig 10 reveals a clear U-shaped FID profile over the diffusion timesteps: at the very beginning (steps 1–2), high FID values (~120–90) indicate that the model’s outputs are overly smooth and lack the necessary textural detail; as the process advances into mid-range steps (4–6), FID reaches its minimum (~45), signifying the sweet spot where both coarse anatomical structures and fine ulcer textures are most faithfully reconstructed; beyond this window (steps 8–10), FID climbs again (~70–120), reflecting under-refinement of key features. This timestep-wise analysis reveals that sampling around timesteps 4–6 yields the most perceptually realistic images, suggesting that focusing training or early-stopping criteria within this phase can improve the perceptual realism and distributional consistency of generated progression-like DFU outputs.

sec.title: 5.4 Qualitative visual comparisons
sec.p: The qualitative visual comparisons in this subsection are presented as technical visual inspection outputs and should not be interpreted as formal clinician-rated assessment.

sec.title: 5.4.1 SSIM overview.
sec.p: The SSIM values over the three timesteps show a quantitative measure of the model’s performance across the pseudo-stages corresponding to the severity levels, as displayed in Table 6. The lowest SSIM value is 0.674 for timestep 1, suggesting that the synthetic reconstruction has the greatest difficulty at the very beginning, possibly because of the more complicated edge structures and texture gradient variations in the early wound formation. However, Timestep 2 has the best SSIM (0.804), indicating that the model performs better in terms of capturing the intermediate wound characteristics, which may be due to the fact that these stages contain more stable and less complex textures. Some loss of fidelity is seen in timestep 3 with a moderate SSIM of 0.726, especially in reproducing the deep central granulation and subtle surface variations typical of more advanced wounds. These findings, combined, indicate that the model has a good overall performance and can capture fine structural details and textural nuances well, but there is room for improvement in the early and advanced ulcer stages, where the performance was not as good. The values of SSIM calculated at each time step are used to indicate structural consistency with pseudo-progression references and are not the same as the accuracy of longitudinal progression.

sec.title: 5.4.2 Grid montage: Real vs. Synthetic vs. Difference.
sec.p: The grid montage provides a step-by-step visualization of the proposed model’s ability to synthesize realistic progression-like DFU images, in an intuitive way. In all three timesteps, the synthetic outputs are able to accurately replicate the overall shape, wound size and general tissue structure of the real images. The absolute-difference heatmaps (right column), however, show areas of difference that are important for clinical interpretation. In particular, the model tends to damp down sharp edges of wound lesions and subtle variations in texture, resulting in higher error signals at the edges of lesions and at areas of slight tissue variation. For instance, the edges of the synthetic ulcer are not as sharp as those of the real image in Timestep 1. In Timestep 3, the central area of the wound is only very roughly approximated, while the rich textural details are somewhat lost. These spatial error patterns emphasize the need to improve the details of high-frequency reconstruction and preservation of edges. Overall, the montage suggests a good accuracy of the diffusion model in the global aspect and provides explicit knowledge about the points where the model can be improved on a micro aspect to make it more accurate, as shown in Fig 11.

sec.title: 5.4.3 Texture detail zoom-ins.
sec.p: The generated progression-like DFU images are assessed visually in terms of the model’s ability to preserve micro-level texture details in the images through the 4 × magnified crop in Fig 12. The real image patch exhibits better definition of the ulcer margins, higher local contrast and better visibility of fine scale surface irregularities. Compared to the synthetic patch, the overall ulcer pattern and overall intensity gradient remain intact, but there is some smoothing of high frequency details, especially around the edge of the ulcer and areas of low tissue heterogeneity. The observation suggests that the proposed diffusion framework is more successful in maintaining the morphology of the ulcers at the macro level, rather than the very fine microstructural texture patterns. This over smoothing is a significant technical constraint as the transitions in texture at the edges could affect the visual interpretation of the appearance patterns that resemble granulation, slough and necrosis. Hence, the images created should not be regarded as complete substitutes of real high-resolution images of wounds, especially in the case of fine texture of the boundaries or subtle variation in the tissues. The zoom-in analysis is also presented to explicitly point out this limitation and to provide a guideline for future model refinement. Texture preserving techniques like frequency-aware loss functions, multi-scale patch-level supervision, boundary-aware conditioning, and edge-preserving post-refinement modules should be added in future iterations of the framework. The additions could enhance the retention of details that occur at high frequencies and preserve the overall structural consistency that is provided by the current model. Therefore, the proposed framework is supported by a balanced interpretation as presented in Fig 12, which shows that the framework is morphologically well preserved on a global scale, and yet there is a need for further refinement in terms of micro-texture preservation.

caption.title: High-resolution zoom: real vs synthetic micro-texture details.

sec.p: This smoothing effect is thus not considered as a small visual artefact, but as a major limitation in the present texture-aware framework with respect to texture preservation. In the current model, this is partially solved by explicitly conditioning the texture in the LBP stage, using deep perceptual features to guide the model, focusing on ulcer regions using cross-attention, and enforcing feature consistency loss. These components, however, better preserve the morphology at a global scale and the organization of the mid-level texture than very high-frequency microstructural detail, as seen in the zoom-in analysis. The finding indicates that texture awareness at conditioning level only is not enough for achieving the full recovery of texture at boundary level. Thus, future extensions should include explicit high-frequency texture constraints including frequency-domain reconstruction loss, Laplacian pyramid loss, boundary-aware texture supervision and local patch-discriminator refinement. The additions would directly address the smoothing effect seen in Fig 12 and enhance the texture preserving ability of the framework.

sec.title: 5.5 Attention overlay on progression-like synthetic output
sec.p: The attention overlay in Fig 13 is essential to understand the spatial attention of the diffusion model in the synthetic DFU generation. This heatmap is based on the edge-based saliency signals and emphasizes the border of the ulcer as well as the central necrotic core with high intensity, and the healthy tissue is not given much attention. This spatial concentration implies that the model emphasizes the high-frequency textural and structural information closely associated with the morphology of ulcers, instead of the irrelevant background pattern. This focused attention gives initial evidence of interpretability; the highlighted regions match the regions of interest in the image, such as the margins and mid-body of the ulcer. Furthermore, the uniform localization of attention in various regions is helpful for the robustness and interpretability of the model, which facilitates transparent examination of the model behaviour. The visualization shows that when synthesizing DFU images that are more like progressions, the model puts emphasis on visually relevant ulcer regions, which is a confirmation that the model’s outputs are not only superficially realistic, but also supported by feature learning that is visually and texturally relevant to the ulcer region.

sec.title: 5.6 Severity-conditioned texture dynamics heatmap on baseline ulcer image
sec.p: Fig 14 presents a severity-conditioned texture variation heatmap overlaid on the baseline ulcer image to show plausible regions of texture variation associated with the severity of the image. The aim of this visualization is to present a meaningful representation of the texture variation of the ulcer region, derived from the model, but keeping the anatomical context of the original image. Red-to-yellow areas in the heatmap represent relatively greater texture variation associated with severity, while blue-to-cyan areas represent relatively less texture variation associated with severity. This color-coded depiction allows visualization of the extent of localization of texture changes in the proposed framework during DFU synthesis of progression. In the case presented, the inner edges of the central ulcer bed and the surrounding inner edges of the ulcerated area are more texturally varied, indicating visually high change areas in the ulcer bed. The regions could be important for future clinically validated interpretation as central wound areas and margins of the ulcers may contain relevant visual cues that are important for tissue heterogeneity, surface irregularity and variation in appearance associated with the severity of the ulcer. The highlighted areas, however, do not necessarily represent clinical risk areas, areas of actual tissue degradation, or the actual areas of treatment. The heatmap is a model-based representation of appearance variation associated with severity and not clinically proven wound progression. The visualization is thus conceived as an exploratory research product to investigate model behavior and to gain insight into the spatial representation of the changes in texture for severity conditions. It could assist in a qualitative evaluation of whether the model captures the ulcer areas that are relevant to the image, rather than non-relevant background areas. Concurrently, care should be taken when interpreting this heatmap as it is not based on the longitudinal ground truth progression data or on prospective clinical outcome validation. Thus, the severity-conditioned texture dynamics heatmap should not be regarded as a clinically validated decision support tool. Do not use for debridement planning, patient counselling, treatment selection or for any type of clinical intervention without formal clinical validation. It is currently used as an exploratory visualizer, technical interpretability and analysis of severity-related texture variation in the proposed synthesis framework for progression. Future studies should confirm such heatmap outputs with longitudinal cohorts of DFUs, more clinician-centered assessments, and studies with outcomes to establish the clinical relevance of these visual patterns.

The regions shown are not considered to be validated evidence of actual tissue status, biological progression or clinical risk. Therefore, the overlay should not be used as a replacement for direct clinical assessment, clinical expertise or accepted protocols for wound assessment. sec.title: 5.8 Ablation study results on model components
sec.p: The descriptive ablation results in Table 7 show that the full model produced the most favorable observed metric values among the evaluated configurations, with SSIM of 0.851 ± 0.020, FID of 44.33 ± 5.02, TCS of 0.79 ± 0.04, and GTFS of 0.76 ± 0.05. Removal of texture conditioning was associated with lower observed SSIM, TCS, and GTFS values and a higher FID, suggesting reduced preservation of local micro-textural characteristics and granulation-related appearance patterns. Removal of cross-attention also showed lower SSIM and higher FID values relative to the full model, indicating reduced structural similarity and distributional alignment. The configuration without either module produced the least favorable observed values across all four metrics. Taken together, these descriptive trends suggest that texture conditioning and cross-attention both contribute to the observed performance of the complete framework. However, because formal statistical significance testing was not performed, the observed differences should be interpreted as comparative trends on the fixed held-out test set rather than statistically established between-model effects.

sec.title: 5.9 External dataset validation and cross‑dataset generalization analysis
5.9.1 External dataset description.
sec.p: To further strengthen the robustness and generalisability of the proposed texture‑aware conditional diffusion framework, an additional external validation was conducted using an independent diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) image dataset obtained from Kaggle [31]. The external dataset contains 810 training images with labels, 200 validation images with labels and 200 test images, acquired in heterogeneous clinical conditions such as different light conditions, acquisition devices and ulcer appearance. This external validation was added in particular to address concerns regarding overfitting and limited data generalization. The primary dataset has only 493 DFU images, so the evaluation of the proposed framework using an independent dataset is more representative of the ability of the algorithm to learn the patterns of ulcer texture and morphology rather than the visual characteristics of the dataset.

More importantly, this external dataset was not used during the training, fine tuning or hyperparameter selection of the model, which allowed an unbiased evaluation of cross-dataset performance. The labels given in the dataset were only used for severity aligned grouping and evaluation and not as the temporal or longitudinal ground truth. This design is consistent with the pseudo progression paradigm used in the primary dataset and allows for meaningful external validation when there is a domain shift as demonstrated in Fig 16.

caption.title: Sample images from external dataset.

sec.title: 5.9.2 External validation protocol.
sec.p: No retraining or adaptation was performed for the trained diffusion model on the external dataset and it was directly used for inference in a zero-shot setting. To guarantee methodological consistency in processing all images, the same pipeline of pre-processing was implemented, as described in Section 3.2, that consisted of resolution standardization, background suppression, texture enhancement and histogram normalization. A progression of synthetic images was created for each of the external input images with the same diffusion timestep setting used in the main experiments. The quantitative evaluation was done by SSIM, FID, Texture Consistency Score (TCS), and Granulation Tissue Fidelity Score (GTFS) and thus could be directly compared to the results reported in the primary dataset. In addition, qualitative visual inspections were performed to evaluate the plausibility of structural coherence, texture continuity and progression in cross dataset conditions.

sec.title: 5.9.3 Quantitative results on external dataset.
sec.p: The quantitative results in Table 8 show that the proposed framework is stable and competitive when tested on a new DFU dataset. Compared with the primary test set, a modest reduction in SSIM from 0.851 ± 0.020 to 0.801 ± 0.028 and in TCS from 0.79 ± 0.04 to 0.75 ± 0.05 was observed under external domain shift. The FID score is 38.7, which also suggests a high similarity between the distribution of generated images and the real image distribution, thereby demonstrating that the diffusion model can be applied to other data sources. The small drop in SSIM and TCS for the external dataset shows some sensitivity to domain shift, as one would expect in the absence of much training data. The proposed framework, however, is able to preserve reasonable values of FID, TCS and GTFS across the datasets, indicating that the framework is not purely memorisation of the primary dataset. The external dataset results also offer some initial insights into the generalizability of TCS and GTFS. Both scores dropped marginally from the primary data, but remained in a consistent range, suggesting that these scores can be used to measure consistency of appearance under domain shift in terms of texture and granulation. However, validation in larger multi-centre DFU datasets is needed for these metrics to be used as generalizable evaluation metrics.

sec.title: 5.9.4 Qualitative cross‑dataset analysis.
sec.p: The external dataset was used to generate synthetic outputs that resemble progression; as shown in Fig 17, the boundaries of the ulcers, the central morphology of the wounds and the surrounding tissue context are preserved consistently across the progression-like synthetic outputs. Changes in progression appear to be spatially coherent, and there are gradual changes in texture rather than abrupt or unrealistic changes. Minor smoothing of higher frequency texture details, especially at the margins of ulcers are seen in some cases, as observed in the primary dataset, but the overall biological plausibility and clinical interpretability is preserved.
