sec.title: 5.9.5 Implications for longitudinal validation.
sec.p: While the external validation results indicate the robustness of the proposed severity-conditioned synthesis framework across the different datasets, they may not be taken as evidence of true temporal prediction. The external dataset also does not have patient-level longitudinal follow-up, so the validation process also only supports the generalisability of progression-like visual synthesis under domain shift, but not chronological wound forecasting. While there is good cross dataset generalisability from external validation, this is not a substitute for true longitudinal validation. The primary and external datasets do not have patient level multi visit follow up images for direct evaluation of real temporal disease evolution. The pseudo progression framework used in this study is thus a weak form of progression, rather than a temporal predictor, such as visual transitions.

Longitudinal DFU cohorts in the future will need to be linked to clinically documented timepoints of follow up to directly assess temporal consistency, healing trajectories and clinical concordance, which can be validated. Nevertheless, the current external validation provides strong evidence that the proposed framework forms a reliable methodological foundation for future longitudinal modelling. Similarly, SSIM, FID, TCS, and GTFS values obtained during external validation indicate cross-dataset fidelity and texture consistency only. They do not confirm longitudinal progression accuracy because no patient-specific longitudinal ground truth was available in the external dataset.

sec.title: 5.10 Statistical considerations
sec.p: Formal statistical significance testing between models was not performed due to the limited size of the held-out test set and the deterministic nature of the fixed data split. Instead, performance was reported using mean ± standard deviation across evaluation metrics, complemented by consistent performance trends observed across baseline comparisons, ablation studies, progression-stage analysis, and external dataset validation. This multi-faceted evaluation strategy was adopted to provide robust evidence of performance stability while avoiding potentially misleading significance estimates on small test samples. Additionally, because the pseudo-stages are derived from cross-sectional severity grouping rather than actual longitudinal follow-up, statistical comparisons are interpreted in terms of synthetic image fidelity and severity-conditioned consistency. They are not intended to validate real temporal prediction accuracy. True progression accuracy can only be assessed using longitudinal DFU cohorts with repeated imaging of the same patients over clinically documented follow-up intervals. Accordingly, terms implying formal statistical superiority or significance are avoided in the interpretation of the baseline and ablation comparisons. Differences in SSIM, PSNR, FID, TCS, and GTFS are reported as descriptive numerical trends on the fixed held-out test set and should not be interpreted as statistically significant between-model effects.

The absence of longitudinal future-state images also limits the interpretation of image-quality metrics. SSIM and PSNR assess similarity to severity-aligned pseudo-progression references, while FID assesses similarity to the overall real-image distribution. These metrics are useful for evaluating synthetic image quality but cannot determine whether a generated output matches the actual longitudinal future state of an ulcer. Therefore, the reported quantitative results should be interpreted as evidence of image fidelity and severity-conditioned consistency, not as validation of longitudinal progression accuracy.

sec.title: 6. Discussion
sec.p: This study presents a texture-aware conditional diffusion framework for generating severity-conditioned progression-like synthetic images of diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) from a single input image. The framework should be interpreted as a weakly supervised synthesis approach rather than a true temporal prediction model, because the available datasets consist of independent single-timepoint images without patient-specific longitudinal follow-up. By arranging cross-sectional images into severity-aligned pseudo-stages, the model learns population-level visual transitions associated with ulcer morphology and texture, rather than chronological wound dynamics within the same patient. The pseudo-progression assumption also has important physiological limitations. Diabetic foot ulcer evolution is not governed by visual severity alone, but is influenced by patient-specific biological and clinical factors, including vascular status, neuropathy, infection burden, glycaemic control, pressure redistribution, treatment response, wound care interventions, and systemic comorbidities. Since these factors were not available as longitudinal clinical variables in the dataset, the constructed pseudo-stages cannot represent the actual physiological trajectory of a specific ulcer. In addition, true wound progression may be non-linear, reversible, treatment-dependent, or interrupted by healing and deterioration events. Therefore, the generated outputs should be interpreted as severity-conditioned advanced severity-state visualizations rather than precise temporal forecasts of future ulcer evolution. For future longitudinal extension, the proposed framework can be adapted using a staged validation strategy. First, the current model may be retained as a cross-sectional severity-conditioned pretraining model for learning general ulcer texture and morphology representations. Second, the model should be fine-tuned on longitudinal DFU cohorts containing repeated images of the same ulcers across clinically documented follow-up intervals. In such a setting, pseudo-stage labels should be replaced or supplemented with actual follow-up targets, visit intervals, and available clinical covariates. Third, patient-level data splitting should be used to prevent leakage across training, validation, and testing subsets. Finally, generated follow-up images should be compared with real follow-up images using image-fidelity metrics, texture-preservation metrics, blinded clinician assessment, temporal consistency analysis, and clinical concordance with healing or deterioration outcomes. This future framework would allow direct assessment of whether severity-conditioned progression-like synthesis can be extended toward true patient-specific temporal modelling.

The best-performing variant achieves an SSIM of 0.851 ± 0.020, PSNR of 24.76 ± 1.12 dB, and FID of 44.33 ± 5.02, compared with the GAN baseline (SSIM: 0.782 ± 0.031, PSNR: 21.98 ± 1.56 dB, FID: 59.13 ± 6.59) and the VAE baseline (SSIM: 0.738 ± 0.038, PSNR: 19.63 ± 1.83 dB, FID: 69.77 ± 7.44). Additionally, the proposed Texture Consistency Score (TCS) and Granulation Tissue Fidelity Score (GTFS) further corroborate the biological realism of the generated images, with scores of 0.79 ± 0.04 and 0.76 ± 0.05 respectively, showing a good preservation of microstructural detail and plausible representation of granulation-related appearance variation. Ablation studies show the complementary benefits of texture conditioning and cross-attention. Explicit texture encoding for DFU synthesis is important as the removing texture conditioning reduced SSIM to 0.802 ± 0.027 and increased FID to 56.41 ± 6.18, with lower TCS 0.69 ± 0.06 and GTFS 0.63 ± 0.07. . Without cross-attention, SSIM is 0.815 ± 0.023, FID 52.87 ± 5.91, TCS 0.72 ± 0.05, and GTFS 0.66 ± 0.06, indicating that cross-attention helps to align conditioning signals and generated content in space. The variant with neither mechanism is most degraded (SSIM 0.778 ± 0.030, FID 61.95 ± 7.02, TCS 0.65 ± 0.07, GTFS 0.59 ± 0.08), suggesting that both mechanisms are important for good progression-like synthesis. Additionally, the progression-stage analysis shows that the model can capture the appearance variation from the beginning to the end of the progression, with SSIM scores of 0.674, 0.804, and 0.726 for the first, second, and third stage, respectively. Overall, the final full-model evaluation yielded an SSIM of 0.851 ± 0.020, FID of 44.33 ± 5.02, TCS of 0.79 ± 0.04, and GTFS of 0.76 ± 0.05, consistently reflecting structural fidelity, distributional similarity, and preservation of severity-related appearance characteristics across the reported analyses. However, without the ground truth longitudinal future images, SSIM, PSNR and FID cannot directly assess the accuracy of longitudinal progression. The three metrics: SSIM, PSNR, and FID, measure structural and pixel-level similarity to pseudo-progression references, and similarity between generated images and the current DFU image distribution, respectively. These metrics thus help to evaluate the quality of synthetic images and their realism in distribution, but do not prove that the synthetic image is the actual future state of a particular ulcer over time.

Additional support for potential clinical utility is provided by interpretability analyses. However, clinical implications of these findings should be interpreted cautiously. The main metrics used in the present validation are image similarity metrics, distributional realism metrics, texture-based scores, ablation analysis and qualitative visual plausibility inspection. These assessments are helpful in determining the technical quality of images and initial visual plausibility but they are not enough to determine the effectiveness of clinical decision support. The suggested framework has not yet been proven in potential clinical settings, has not been tested for impact on clinical decision making, and has not been correlated with patient-level outcomes like healing rate, infection prevention, or amputation reduction. Attention overlays and risk heat maps always focus on clinically relevant areas of ulcer (the central wound bed and peri-ulcer margins) but not on other background structures. The high-change regions found in the framework often coincide with the ulcer regions that are visually relevant such as necrosis-like, slough-like or granulation-like tissue appearance. The outputs should however be used as exploratory visualisations and should not be used as a guide for planning debridement, dressing selection or offloading without prospective clinical validation. These visual explanations will help future exploration of interpretable wound assessment workflows by providing intuitive, case-specific summaries of visual trajectories and regions that are likely to be associated with the severity of wounds, and should be monitored more carefully. An external validation was conducted on an independent dataset of DFU images obtained from Kaggle, that includes labelled images collected under varying clinical conditions in order to increase the robustness of the assessment. The proposed model was tested on this dataset in a zero-shot learning scenario without retraining or hyperparameter tuning and the same metrics as used for the main dataset. The external evaluation resulted in an SSIM of 0.801 ± 0.028, FID of 38.7 ± 4.9, TCS of 0.75 ± 0.05, and GTFS of 0.72 ± 0.06 which shows that it performs well under domain shift and only a small degradation compared to the primary test set. Qualitative examples showed that the morphology of the global foot and the shape of the ulcer remained unchanged, and that any changes that seemed to be progressing were limited to the ulcer bed and margins. These results indicate that the framework is not only learning appearance patterns of the datasets, but also learning transferable representations of ulcer texture and morphology that are able to generalize across different clinical image distributions. The results of the external validation of the proposed framework, presented in Section 5.9, also support the generalisability of the framework under different imaging conditions and ulcer presentations. The relatively small size of the primary data set is a factor to consider in interpreting the results. Typically, diffusion-based generative models work better with larger and more diverse datasets, so that using 493 images might make them more susceptible to overfitting to the imaging conditions of the dataset. This concern was partially mitigated by data augmentation, fixed validation protocols, ablation analysis and zero-shot external dataset validation. The external validation results show a structural and texture similarity under domain shift, but further multi-institutional validation is needed.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, both the primary and external datasets lack patient-level longitudinal image sequences with clinically documented follow-up time points. The pseudo-progression stages used in this work are therefore derived from severity-aligned groupings rather than true temporal observations. As a result, the framework should be interpreted as modelling progression-like visual transitions under weak supervision, rather than providing definitive temporal predictions of individual patient trajectories. Second, zoom-in analyses reveal some loss of very fine texture elements, particularly at ulcer boundaries, indicating that additional texture-preserving mechanisms such as frequency-aware generators, multi-scale refinement modules, or hybrid loss functions that emphasise high-frequency content may be beneficial. Third, although external validation supports cross-dataset generalisability, the datasets considered remain limited in size and geographic diversity, and performance may be influenced by differences in imaging protocols, lighting conditions, and patient characteristics. Although the proposed diffusion framework preserves global ulcer morphology and overall texture continuity, the zoom-in analysis in Fig 12 shows residual over-smoothing of high-frequency micro-textural details near wound boundaries. This limitation is particularly important for a texture-aware synthesis framework, because fine boundary-level texture transitions may influence the visual distinction between granulation-like, slough-like, and necrosis-like appearance patterns. The current architecture partially mitigates texture degradation through LBP-based texture conditioning, deep perceptual features, cross-attention-guided ulcer-region focusing, and feature consistency constraints. However, after iterative denoising these components do not fully recover the very fine high-frequency structures completely.

This is a limitation that needs to be addressed in future work specifically with refinement strategies that are frequency- and boundary-aware. The inclusion of a Focal Frequency Loss would help to penalize the missing high-frequency spectral components, and would encourage reconstruction of the fine surface irregularities, the sharpness of the wound edges and the subtle variations of the local tissue. Likewise, high-pass filtering the images before evaluating the discriminator would add a high-pass-filter guided adversarial loss, which would require the adversarial loss to be concerned with retaining micro-texture, as well as with global photorealism. Furthermore, Laplacian pyramid loss, multi-scale patch-level supervision, boundary-aware conditioning and an edge-preserving post-refinement module may be added to further enhance the preservation of high-frequency details. These additions are anticipated to help decrease smoothing without compromising the global structural fidelity that is already attained by the existing model. This study is mainly methodological and technically validates the methods with publicly available datasets. Structured usability studies with wound care specialists will be conducted in the future to assess the interpretability, clinical usefulness, and value of the decision support in real-life wound care management.

Future studies should focus on the inclusion of longitudinal DFU cohorts in which patients are followed across a number of visits with the same imaging techniques and comprehensive clinical annotations. These types of datasets would allow for direct assessment of temporal consistency, progression accuracy and clinical concordance, as well as calibration of progression like synthesis to actual healing or deterioration trajectories. Further increases in training and validation data to larger multi-institutional datasets would increase robustness and reduce potential biases from single-centre or single-source imagery. The explicit inclusion of clinical covariates (e.g., perfusion status, markers of infection, comorbidities) can also enable the modelling of the progression patterns in images and systemic risk factors together. The proposed texture-aware diffusion framework offers a methodological basis for the severity-conditioned progression-like visualization of DFU appearances. It should be used for technical synthesis and exploratory interpretation only, however, until larger longitudinal data sets, clinician-centred validation, and prospective outcome-based assessment are available. The proposed framework shows consistent improvement on various evaluation measures, but there are a few shortcomings in terms of statistical robustness that need to be recognized. Large annotated DFU datasets are not available, which makes patient-wise splitting and k-fold cross validation difficult, especially for the diffusion based generative models, which are computationally heavy. For this reason, in this study a fixed split strategy was used to guarantee the same and fair comparison of the models. In the future, more statistically sound validation methods will be investigated, such as cross validation and uncertainty aware evaluation, when more and more diverse DFU data sets are available. These will further build confidence in the generalisability of the models and their clinical applicability.

sec.p: The results of the proposed texture-aware conditional diffusion framework are summarized in Table 9, which compares it with other methods. The models based on CNN or hybrid models are able to get good classification and segmentation accuracy, but they mainly work on static evaluation instead of progression-like severity-conditioned synthesis. The proposed method, on the contrary, enables the synthesis of a progression-like DFU from a single image, with high structural fidelity (SSIM: 0.851), excellent photorealism (FID: 44.33) and good preservation of biological texture (TCS: 0.79, GTFS: 0.76). Based on these results, the proposed method is expected to be a valuable methodological contribution for the synthesis of diabetic foot ulcers with progression and further validation is required to make generalization and clinical applicability statements.

sec.title: 6.2 Limitations and future validation requirements
sec.p: A central limitation of the present study is the absence of true longitudinal diabetic foot ulcer image sequences. The datasets used in this work consist of independent single-timepoint images rather than repeated follow-up images of the same patients. Therefore, the pseudo-progression stages were constructed using cross-sectional severity-related visual cues, such as ulcer size, depth, granulation prevalence, and necrotic coverage, rather than actual temporal wound trajectories. As a result, the proposed framework does not learn genuine patient-specific temporal progression dynamics. The generated outputs should therefore be interpreted as severity-conditioned progression-like visualizations, not as deterministic predictions of an individual ulcer’s future clinical state.

A related limitation is that the pseudo-progression paradigm effectively represents severity-conditioned appearance interpolation across different patients rather than true temporal modelling within the same patient. This limitation arises because the ordinal pseudo-stages are derived from cross-sectional DFU images belonging to independent cases, not from repeated follow-up observations of the same ulcer. The pseudo-stage labels were not treated as clinician-validated annotations; no formal clinician-led annotation or adjudication protocol was used to establish longitudinal or diagnostic ground truth for these groupings. Therefore, the term progression-like is used throughout this study to indicate severity-conditioned synthetic visualization under limited longitudinal data availability, not actual future progression prediction. True patient-specific temporal progression prediction would require longitudinal DFU cohorts containing repeated images of the same ulcers across clinically documented follow-up intervals.

Another limitation is related to the clinical validation of the generated images. The present evaluation is primarily based on image-quality and visual-fidelity metrics, including SSIM, FID, TCS, and GTFS, along with qualitative visual plausibility inspection. Although these evaluations are useful for assessing structural similarity, distributional realism, texture preservation, and preliminary visual plausibility, they are not sufficient to establish real-world clinical decision-support effectiveness. These metrics cannot determine whether the generated images improve diagnostic safety, treatment selection, healing outcomes, infection prevention, or amputation-risk reduction.

A further limitation is that no formal clinician-led expert validation was conducted in the present study. The qualitative assessment was limited to visual plausibility inspection and did not involve blinded review by wound-care specialists, Likert-scale scoring, or inter-rater reliability analysis. Therefore, the findings should be interpreted as technical evidence of synthetic image fidelity and visual plausibility rather than clinician-validated clinical realism. Future studies should include blinded assessment by multiple wound-care specialists, structured rating criteria, inter-rater agreement analysis, and comparison with established wound assessment standards.

A further limitation concerns the interpretation of SSIM, PSNR, and FID in the absence of true longitudinal future-state images. These metrics are not suitable for assessing the longitudinal future state of a particular ulcer. However, SSIM and PSNR measure similarity to pseudo-progression images that are matched to severity, and FID measures distributional similarity to the current DFU image database. Thus, the reported metrics should be treated as measures of the image fidelity of the synthetic images and the realism of the datasets and not as measures of the accuracy of the longitudinal progressions.

The size and type of publicly available datasets are also limiting the study. While the number of images was limited by pre-processing, augmentation, regularization and external validation to address overfitting issues, 493 images are still a relatively small dataset to train a diffusion-based generative model. However, the model could be affected by the imaging characteristics of the dataset, such as lighting, acquisition conditions, placement of the wound and the way the ulcers are presented. Thus, the findings should be considered as preliminary evidence of technical feasibility and cross-dataset robustness, not as evidence of generalizability. Future studies should use and validate the framework on larger, multi-centre DFU datasets that include a wider variety of imaging devices, patient populations, skin tones, wound locations, and clinical severity.

Patient-level identifiers were not available; therefore, patient-wise data splitting could not be performed. This may limit the ability to fully assess generalization across independent patients. In addition, the datasets may not capture the full diversity of diabetic foot ulcer presentations, imaging devices, lighting conditions, skin tones, wound locations, infection states, vascular status, and clinical treatment histories. Although external dataset validation was included to evaluate cross-dataset robustness, such validation does not replace longitudinal or prospective clinical validation.

A further technical limitation is the partial loss of fine micro-textural details observed in some generated images, particularly near ulcer boundaries. Since edge-level granulation, slough, and necrotic transitions may be clinically important, future versions of the framework should incorporate texture-preserving strategies such as frequency-aware loss functions, multi-scale refinement modules, boundary-aware conditioning, and patch-level supervision to improve high-frequency detail preservation.

A further limitation concerns the proposed Texture Consistency Score and Granulation Tissue Fidelity Score. Although these metrics provide task-specific information about micro-texture preservation and granulation-related appearance fidelity, they are newly introduced and should be interpreted as supplementary exploratory measures rather than established evaluation standards. Their reliability was supported only indirectly through consistency with ablation trends and external dataset performance. Future studies should validate these metrics against larger clinician-annotated datasets, multiple wound-care specialists, inter-rater agreement analysis, and established wound assessment criteria before they can be considered broadly reliable or generalizable.

Overall, the proposed framework should be considered a methodological and exploratory visualization approach at this stage. It provides a foundation for severity-conditioned progression-like diabetic foot ulcer synthesis, but it should not be regarded as a validated clinical decision-support system. Future studies should validate the framework using longitudinal DFU cohorts with repeated patient-specific images, larger multi-institutional datasets, blinded clinician studies, prospective workflow testing, and outcome-based clinical evaluation before clinical applicability or deployment can be claimed.

sec.title: 7. Conclusion and future scope
sec.p: This study proposes a texture-aware conditional diffusion model for synthesizing severity-conditioned, progression-like diabetic foot ulcer images from a single RGB input image. The proposed approach combines hybrid texture encoding using local binary patterns and deep perceptual features with cross-attention enhanced diffusion modelling, thus addressing key limitations of existing progression-like ulcer synthesis techniques. The framework does not attempt any patient-specific temporal forecasting as there is no time-series data of follow-up images. The study, however, shows that weakly supervised pseudo-progression modelling can produce plausible visual transitions that are aligned with the severity of the disease and retain clinically relevant texture and morphology.

The quantitative evaluation demonstrated favorable performance across multiple image-quality measures. The proposed model achieved an SSIM of 0.851 ± 0.020, PSNR of 24.76 ± 1.12 dB, and FID of 44.33 ± 5.02, corresponding to higher observed SSIM and PSNR and lower FID values than the evaluated GAN and VAE baselines. The Texture Consistency Score (TCS: 0.79 ± 0.04) and Granulation Tissue Fidelity Score (GTFS: 0.76 ± 0.05) were also computed to demonstrate the model’s capacity to retain fine-grained texture and appearance patterns associated with granulation. The ablation studies further demonstrated the importance of the texture-conditioning and cross-attention modules, where their removal led to a decrease in structural fidelity, texture consistency, and distributional realism. The progression-stage analysis further confirmed the ability of the model to portray severity-aligned pseudo-stages with structural consistency at timesteps 1, 2 and 3 with SSIM values of 0.674, 0.804 and 0.726, respectively.

The quantitative findings should be interpreted cautiously. In the absence of true longitudinal future-state images, SSIM, PSNR and FID can be used to assess the fidelity of synthetic images, the consistency of their structure, and the realism of their distribution, but not the accuracy of longitudinal progression. Therefore, these metrics should not be interpreted as indicators of whether a generated image accurately represents the future appearance of an individual patient’s ulcer. Longitudinal datasets will be needed in the future to determine if the images generated are progression-like images of real patients. Likewise, severity-conditioned risk heatmaps and attention overlays are not intended as clinical decision support outputs, but rather as exploratory visualizations.

Pseudo-progression stages were derived from predefined cross-sectional visual severity cues rather than longitudinal imaging data. Because these ordinal groupings are based on appearance characteristics rather than patient-specific temporal observations, they may not fully represent the biological complexity or temporal variability of diabetic foot ulcer progression. Moreover, small loss of micro-level textural details was noticed in zoomed areas, suggesting the requirement of texture optimized refinement modules or loss functions emphasizing high-frequency detail preservation. Another key constraint of diffusion-based DFU synthesis is the relatively small size of the primary data set. While data augmentation, regularization, fixed evaluation protocols, ablation analysis, and external dataset validation were employed to mitigate overfitting issues, the remaining 493 images are still relatively small for training a diffusion-based generative model. However, the model could be influenced by specific characteristics of the data, such as the lighting conditions, acquisition parameters, position of the wounds, and patterns of ulcer presentation.

The cross-dataset robustness was further validated with an external dataset, which helped alleviate the risk of memorizing the primary dataset. But this does not mean that this is a substitute for a more comprehensive multi-institutional assessment. Longitudinal image sequences of DFU taken at various clinical follow-up visits should be included in future studies to assess the temporal consistency, the patient-specific wound trajectory, and the accuracy of the longitudinal progression. In addition, larger multi-institutional DFU image collections are needed to minimize the risk of overfitting, increase the robustness over imaging conditions, and enhance the basis for assessing the generalization of diffusion-based DFU synthesis models.

The incorporation of multimodal data, such as thermal imaging, 3D surface scans, and clinical data (e.g., vascular status, infection markers, treatment history, and comorbidities) would also be valuable for future research. This information can improve the interpretability and severity-aware modelling of the image-based appearance patterns, as well as provide case-specific interpretability by associating image-based appearance patterns with clinically relevant patient factors. This framework would need to be translated into a real-time clinical decision support environment, and validated in a larger clinician-centred evaluation and outcome-based assessment before being deployed in the management of DFU. For future implementations, uncertainty estimation should also be integrated to provide information on the level of confidence of the outputs generated and to enable more confident interpretation of the severity-conditioned progression-like visualization in different clinical imaging settings and datasets. In general, the proposed framework offers a methodological base for severity-conditioned progression-like synthesis, risk-aware visualization and future longitudinal DFU modelling, highlighting the importance of thorough validation before any clinical claims can be made. Future studies should also involve formal validation of TCS and GTFS with larger clinician annotated DFU datasets and existing wound assessment standards to assess the reliability, reproducibility and generalizability of TCS and GTFS. While the pseudo-progression strategy gives an approximation of the severity-conditioned progression with limited availability of longitudinal data, true modelling of the progression over time will require longitudinal DFU datasets with repeated patient-specific images over clinically documented follow-up time.

Reviewer #1: The manuscript presents a novel texture-aware conditional diffusion model for synthetic progression prediction of diabetic foot ulcers (DFU) from single images. The work is technically solid, clinically relevant, and clearly demonstrates innovation through the integration of hybrid texture encoding and cross-attention within the diffusion framework. The introduction of biologically meaningful evaluation metrics (TCS and GTFS), along with ablation studies and expert validation, further strengthens the contribution.
That said, I recommend the following points for revision to further improve the clarity, reproducibility, and impact of the study:

1. Dataset and Validation: The use of pseudo-progression stages is acknowledged as a limitation. Please expand on this in the discussion and, if possible, consider additional datasets or outline a clear pathway toward longitudinal validation.

2. Preservation of Fine Details: The generated images show some smoothing of micro-textural details, particularly at wound edges. Consider implementing or discussing refinement techniques to better retain clinically important structures.

3. Generalizability: The robustness of the model across diverse clinical imaging conditions (lighting, acquisition protocols, patient demographics) should be further addressed, even if only in discussion.
4. Clinical Usability: Expanding expert validation with larger cohorts or usability testing would strengthen the claim of translational potential.
5. Presentation: The methodology section is dense and may benefit from a pipeline flowchart or summary tables to improve readability for readers from clinical backgrounds.
Overall, this is a strong and promising study with high potential for clinical translation. With minor revisions, the manuscript will be suitable for publication in PLOS ONE.
Reviewer #2: 1, Dataset

The study uses only 493 images from a Kaggle dataset with minimal characterization. There is no information about patient demographics, ulcer grade distribution (Wagner/PEDIS classification), wound etiology, imaging protocols, or device specifications. This raises serious concerns about generalizability and potential biases.
Recommendation: Provide comprehensive dataset characterization, Validate on at least one external dataset from a different source to demonstrate generalizability.
2, Methodology

The researchers created "pseudo-progression stages" by grouping different patients' ulcers based on severity rankings rather than tracking actual progression over time. This means the model is learning cross-sectional severity differences between different patients, not actual temporal progression dynamics of individual ulcers.
The model cannot genuinely predict how a specific ulcer will evolve because it has never seen actual progression sequences.
Recommendation: Add a dedicated "Limitations" subsection explicitly acknowledging this fundamental constraint and its implications for clinical applicability.
3, Data incomplete

The paper reports standard deviations but lacks essential statistical details: exact test set sizes, data splitting methodology, statistical significance testing between models, and reproducibility information. It's unclear whether performance differences are statistically significant or whether good results might be due to favorable data splits.

Recommendation: Clearly specify exact numbers for training set size, validation set size, test set size, Describe splitting strategy, Provide complete reproducibility package, like: Model architecture specifications in a table format, Complete hyperparameter settings, and Consider k-fold cross-validation

Reviewer #1: This manuscript presents a texture-aware diffusion framework for generating synthetic future progression of diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) from single images. The topic is timely and relevant, and the proposed integration of texture encoding with conditional diffusion modeling is technically interesting. The manuscript is well structured, and the experimental section includes ablation studies and both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. However, there are several major concerns that need to be addressed before the manuscript can be considered for publication.

First, the most critical issue lies in the definition of “progression prediction.” The dataset used in this study consists of independent single-timepoint images without true longitudinal follow-up. The proposed pseudo-progression strategy, where images are grouped into ordinal stages, does not provide genuine temporal supervision. As a result, the model does not truly learn progression dynamics but rather learns a synthetic ordering. This significantly weakens the core claim of predicting future ulcer progression.

Second, the manuscript makes strong clinical claims (e.g., clinical decision support and biologically realistic progression), which are not sufficiently supported by the presented validation. The evaluation is primarily based on image similarity metrics (SSIM, FID) and a limited expert review involving two specialists. While these are useful, they are insufficient to justify clinical applicability. More rigorous clinical validation or a clearer limitation discussion is required.

Third, the evaluation framework raises concerns. Since no ground-truth future images are available, the use of SSIM and FID does not directly measure predictive accuracy of progression. Instead, these metrics only assess similarity to the existing dataset distribution. This distinction should be clearly acknowledged and discussed.

Fourth, the dataset size (493 images) is relatively small for training a diffusion-based generative model, raising concerns about overfitting and generalization. Additional discussion or validation on external datasets would strengthen the work.

Fifth, the proposed metrics (Texture Consistency Score and Granulation Tissue Fidelity Score) appear to be newly introduced but lack sufficient validation or comparison with established evaluation standards. Their reliability and generalizability should be clarified.
Finally, several novelty claims (e.g., “first study”) appear overstated and should be carefully revised to avoid overclaiming.

In summary, while the proposed framework is technically sound and promising, the manuscript currently overstates its contributions and clinical implications. Addressing the issues related to progression definition, evaluation validity, and claim justification is necessary.
I recommend major revision.
Reviewer #2: 1. "Pseudo-Progression" Paradigm

In Section 3.1 (Phase 1: Data Collection), the authors explicitly state that longitudinal follow-up images were not included, and each image was treated as an independent case. To model progression, Section 3.5 introduces a "pseudo-progression paradigm" where independent images are grouped into ordinal stages based on severity.

Training a diffusion model on cross-sectional images sorted by severity effectively models disease severity interpolation across different patients, rather than true patient-specific temporal progression. While this is a clever workaround for data scarcity, calling it "future progression prediction" is clinically misleading.

The authors must explicitly discuss the physiological limitations of the "pseudo-progression" assumption in the Discussion section. It is highly recommended to reframe the narrative slightly to clarify that the model synthesizes "advanced severity states" rather than precise temporal forecasts, and to propose a concrete framework for how this model could be fine-tuned or validated on true longitudinal cohorts in the future.
2. Missing Quantitative Results from the Expert Clinical Review

In Section 3.6 (Phase 6: Evaluation and Validation), the methodology states that a qualitative validation was performed through an expert review study involving two board-certified wound care specialists. The experts reportedly evaluated 100 images using a 5-point Likert scale, and inter-rater reliability was measured using Cohen’s kappa coefficient.

Despite outlining this rigorous clinical validation protocol in the methodology, the quantitative results of this expert review are entirely absent from Section 5 (Experimental Results). The results section only presents automated metrics (SSIM, FID, TCS, GTFS).

Add a dedicated subsection and table in Section 5 detailing the outcomes of the clinical expert review. Include the mean Likert scores for morphological plausibility, textural accuracy, and clinical realism, as well as the exact Cohen’s kappa score to validate the clinical trustworthiness of the synthetic images.
3. Novel Evaluation Metrics
The paper introduces two highly specific metrics: Texture Consistency Score (TCS) and Granulation Tissue Fidelity Score (GTFS) to validate biological realism.

While Section 5.2 briefly mentions that TCS uses Local Binary Pattern (LBP) histogram analysis, there is no formal mathematical definition or algorithmic formulation provided for either TCS or GTFS in the Methodology (Section 3.6). Without explicit formulas or computation steps, peer researchers cannot reproduce these metrics or validate the claims made in Table 1 and Table 2.
Please, add the mathematical equations and a brief explanation of the algorithms used to compute TCS and GTFS in Section 3.6, similar to how the formulas for SSIM and FID were clearly defined.
4. Mitigating High-Frequency Texture Loss

In Section 5.4.3 and Figure 12, the authors candidly and accurately identify a limitation: the synthetic images suffer from over-smoothing and struggle to reproduce high-frequency microstructural details compared to the real zoom-in patches.
The paper leaves this critical flaw simply as an observation. Given that the entire premise of the paper is a "Texture-Aware" model, addressing this smoothing effect is paramount.

Expand the discussion around Figure 12 and Section 6. Suggest specific architectural or loss-function interventions to solve this. For example, discuss the potential of integrating a Focal Frequency Loss (to penalize missing high-frequency spectrums) or adding a high-pass filter within the adversarial loss block to strictly enforce micro-texture retention in future iterations.
